18633-my-lady-of-doubt:
Randall Parrish published this Revolutionary romance at Chicago in 1911 with A. C. McClurg and Company, pictures by Alonzo Kimball. Its narrator, a soldier fresh from the hard winter at Valley Forge, takes a perilous mission within enemy lines as Sir Henry Clinton takes command. Baron von Steuben's drill and talk of striking again fill the opening campfire scene.

Chapters follow a fete, a mischianza, swords, a blacksmith, minute men, a wagon train capture, and the fight at Monmouth. A lady named Claire, Captain Grant, and General Arnold cross the hero's path, with love set against duty. Parrish keeps the adventure brisk and the history close at hand.
25306-a-dominie-in-doubt:
A. S. Neill's Dominie in Doubt, published in London in 1921, continues the Scottish schoolmaster's story after A Dominie's Log and A Dominie's Dismissed. Neill dedicates the book to Homer Lane, whose first lecture convinced him he knew nothing about education.

Neill visits Macdonald, headmaster of Tarbonny Public School, and argues for free education over analysis. Only an unhappy, moody, thieving, or bullying child needs a teacher's diagnosis, found by watching play and writing. A case study follows Tommy, aged ten, building a Play Town after Caldwell Cook's Play Way. The book is a landmark of progressive schooling.
29817-the-harbor-of-doubt:
Frank Williams, author of The Wilderness Trail, published The Harbor of Doubt in New York in 1915, with pictures by G. W. Gage. Young Captain Code Schofield opens the tale in a deep chair before a fire, pacing as he hears strange talk. He says that if he had died he would have been a hero, but because he lived, there is no crime in history he has not been charged with.

Thirty-one chapters follow an island tale of malice, peril, and proof. A red peril, refugees, a stranger, and Jimmie Thomas's strategy lead to a mystery in the fog bank. Nat Burns shows his hand, trawlers work, and treachery bites. A recovered treasure, a siren, and a fatal letter fix the guilt at last. Elsa's triumph and peace and prosperity close a brisk coastal mystery.
34198-the-will-to-doubt:
Alfred H. Lloyd's 1907 essay The Will to Doubt speaks to the general reader, not only to students of philosophy. Lloyd, a university teacher, argues that doubt now touches morals, work, politics, and faith, and that it must be faced rather than feared.

Ten chapters move from the common view of things to the rise of science, the limits of science, and a doubter's picture of the world. The close joins doubt with belief, sympathy, and a real sense of self, offering doubt as a spur to honest thought instead of a dead end. Lloyd closes with an index, so readers can trace his terms across the argument.
55166-the-unjust-steward-or-the-minister:
Mrs Oliphant's The Unjust Steward, or The Minister's Debt, was published by Lippincott of Philadelphia in 1896 and dedicated, simply, to Denny. Twenty-three chapters carry its family plot, from A Sudden Alarm and After the Funeral through a household controversy, the first marriage in the family, and the Mowbrays. Then the unjust steward once more, Confession, and How to Set It Right.

Chapter one introduces the youngest of a large family. Elsie and Roderick Buchanan are the son and daughter of the Reverend George Buchanan, a minister much esteemed in the city of St Rule. The family calls them the Twins, though a year and a day, as in a fairy tale, lies between them. Elsie is fourteen; Roderick, Rodie in the Scotch love of diminutives, just thirteen. Girl and boy, they are as nearly inseparable as two children can be, alike in height and, in infancy, in looks.
britannica-1911-crown-debt:
Crown Debt is a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains debts owed to the crown in the law of England. Old laws give the crown first claim to be paid from a debtor goods. At common law the crown could seize lands and goods for its debts.

The entry notes how hard it was to tell if land bore such a charge. New acts in time curbed that blind risk for buyers of land. No crown debt now binds land till a court writ is put on record. Plain trade debts to the crown gain the rank of debts by deed. A swift court step named an extent is used to force such sums.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-debt:
A moral theology entry defines debt, in its strict sense, as what is owed to another in justice. In a wider sense it covers gratitude for favours and the rich's duty to the poor, a debt of charity rather than justice. Here the word is taken strictly and ethically, not legally, so debts of honour count as true debts though no court enforces them.

A debt arises from two roots, theologians say. One is wilful unjust damage, which must be made good. The other is possession of another's property, which must be restored. Justice demands each person have his own. The entry then treats payment, excuses, and the bar on entering religious life for those ruined by grave fault through heavy unpaid debt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doubt:
Doubt, from the Latin dubium, is the state in which the mind hangs between two opposed claims and cannot assent to either. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that many claims on one subject may hang in doubt at once, though strictly each doubt pairs a claim with its denial. Doubt stands against certitude, assent without misgiving, and against opinion, assent mixed with misgiving.

Doubt is positive when evidence for and against balances so evenly that choice fails, and negative when it springs from want of enough evidence. Morals and sacraments show the distinction at work: doubtful baptisms and ordinations call for conditional repetition. It points readers to articles on certitude, faith, and scepticism for the wider field.
my-lady-of-doubt:
Randall Parrish wrote this Revolutionary War romance, issued in Chicago in 1911. Alonzo Kimball painted four color pictures for it. Chapter one sends its hero on a perilous mission. He passes within the enemy's lines at once.

The Mischianza, a famed British fête, fills an early chapter. Swords, a blacksmith, and Minute Men crowd the action. A wagon train is captured as threads tangle. Parrish had written My Lady of the North before this. His tales mix spies, balls, and battles with a lady at the center. Doubt about her loyalty drives the hero's risk and the reader's suspense.
